Actinic cheilitis is the most likely diagnosis given its predilection for the vermilion border of the lower lip, chronicity, and frequent lack of symptoms until late stages; it carries high malignant potential and warrants biopsy. Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) must be strongly considered — up to 20% of actinic cheilitis cases progress to SCC, and early invasive or in situ SCC can be entirely asymptomatic. Verruca vulgaris is less common on lips but possible, especially with history of oral contact or immunosuppression; typically more exophytic and shorter duration, but persistence can occur. Lichen planus may present as a white, reticulated, or atrophic plaque on the lip and can be asymptomatic in early or mild forms, though often associated with other mucosal or cutaneous findings. Granuloma fissuratum is a reactive fibrous hyperplasia usually caused by chronic trauma (e.g., ill-fitting dentures), but it’s rare on the lower lip without clear mechanical irritation and typically presents as a firm, pedunculated nodule — less consistent with insidious, painless, non-ulcerated evolution over three months. Absence of additional history (e.g., smoking, UV exposure, immune status, trauma, systemic symptoms) limits further refinement; biopsy remains the gold standard."}

Chronic traumatic ulcers are common but typically show some evidence of healing or recurrence; persistence without tenderness lowers—but does not exclude—this diagnosis. Lichen planus can present as erosive or ulcerative lesions on the lip vermilion, often bilateral and with reticular white striae elsewhere, but isolated persistent single ulcer is less typical. Syphilitic chancre is usually painful and self-limited (3–6 weeks), but atypical presentations in latent or treated syphilis may rarely manifest as chronic painless ulcers—serology is essential to rule out. Mucocele is exceedingly unlikely: it is almost always soft, fluctuant, bluish, and located on the inner lip mucosa—not the vermillion border—and rarely ulcerates or persists unchanged for months without fluctuation or rupture."}
